scenes.narration: The rise of Franklin Pierce was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Franklin Pierce (November 23, 1804 – October 8, 1869) was the 14th president of the United States, serving from 1853 to 1857. A northern Democrat who believed that the abolitionist movement was a fundamental threat to national unity, he alienated anti-slavery groups by signing the Kansas–Nebraska Act and enforcing the Fugitive Slave Act.

Setbacks came early for Franklin Pierce, and the response to them is the real story. Conflict between North and South continued after Pierce's presidency, and, following Abraham Lincoln's victory in the 1860 presidential election, the Southern states seceded, resulting in the American Civil War. Pierce was born in New Hampshire; his father was state governor Benjamin Pierce.

The legacy of Franklin Pierce outlived the circumstances that produced it. He served in the House of Representatives from 1833 until his election to the Senate, where he served from 1837 until his resignation in 1842. His private law practice was a success, and he was appointed New Hampshire's U.S. attorney in 1845.

Few lives travel as far as that of Franklin Pierce, and the distance is the point. Pierce took part in the Mexican–American War as a brigadier general in the United States Army. Democrats saw him as a compromise candidate uniting Northern and Southern interests, and nominated him for president at the 1852 Democratic National Convention.

The childhood of Franklin Pierce contains the adult in small print. King easily defeated the Whig Party ticket of Winfield Scott and William Alexander Graham in the 1852 presidential election. As president, Pierce attempted to enforce neutral standards for civil service while also satisfying the Democratic Party's diverse elements with patronage, an effort that largely failed and turned many in his party against him.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Franklin Pierce — in that order. He was a Young America expansionist who signed the Gadsden Purchase of land from Mexico and led a failed attempt to acquire Cuba from Spain. He signed trade treaties with Britain and Japan and his Cabinet reformed its departments and improved accountability, but political strife during his presidency overshadowed these successes.

The turning point in the life of Franklin Pierce looked like a failure at the time. His popularity declined sharply in the Northern states after he supported the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which nullified the Missouri Compromise, while many Southern whites continued to support him. The act's passage led to violent conflict over the expansion of slavery in the American West.

Every biography of Franklin Pierce has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Pierce's administration was further damaged when several of his diplomats issued the Ostend Manifesto calling for the annexation of Cuba, a document that was roundly criticized. He expected the Democrats to renominate him in the 1856 presidential election, but his bid failed.

The education of Franklin Pierce happened mostly outside any school. His reputation in the North suffered further during the American Civil War as he became a vocal critic of President Lincoln. While Pierce was popular and outgoing, his family life was difficult; his three children died young, and his wife, Jane Pierce, suffered from illness and depression for much of her life.

What Franklin Pierce wanted at the start and what Franklin Pierce got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Their last surviving son was killed in a train accident while the family was traveling, shortly before Pierce's inauguration. A heavy drinker for much of his life, Pierce died in 1869 of cirrhosis.

The defining trait of Franklin Pierce was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. As a result of his support of the South, as well as failing to hold the Union together in time of strife, historians and scholars generally rank Pierce as one of the worst and least memorable U.S. presidents. Franklin Pierce was born on November 23, 1804, in a log cabin in Hillsborough, New Hampshire.

Those who met Franklin Pierce at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. He was a sixth-generation descendant of Thomas Pierce, who had moved to the Massachusetts Bay Colony from Norwich, Norfolk, England, in about 1634. His father Benjamin was a lieutenant in the American Revolutionary War who moved from Chelmsford, Massachusetts, to Hillsborough after the war, purchasing 50 acres (20 ha) of land.

The private years of Franklin Pierce explain the public decades better than any speech. Pierce was the fifth of eight children born to Benjamin and his second wife Anna Kendrick; his first wife Elizabeth Andrews died in childbirth, leaving a daughter. During Pierce's childhood, his father was deeply involved in state politics, while two of his older brothers fought in the War of 1812; public affairs and the military were thus a major influence in his early life.

The family Franklin Pierce came from matters more than the legends admit. Pierce's father placed Pierce in a school at Hillsborough Center in childhood and sent him to the town school in Hancock at age 12. Not fond of schooling, Pierce grew homesick and walked 12 miles (19 km) back to his home one Sunday.

The first real success of Franklin Pierce arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. His father fed him dinner and drove him part of the distance back to school before ordering him to walk the rest of the way in a thunderstorm. Later that year, he transferred to Phillips Exeter Academy to prepare for college.

The last chapter of Franklin Pierce was written long after the fame. By this time, he had built a reputation as a charming student, sometimes prone to misbehavior. In fall 1820, Pierce entered Bowdoin College in Brunswick, Maine, one of 19 freshmen.

The whole life of Franklin Pierce reads like a single decision repeated. He joined the Athenian Society, a progressive literary society, alongside Jonathan Cilley (later elected to Congress) and Nathaniel Hawthorne, with whom he formed lasting friendships. He was the last in his class after two years, but he worked hard to improve his grades and graduated in fifth place in 1824 in a graduating class of 14.

Between the birth and the legend of Franklin Pierce lie the years that actually decide it. Hale enrolled at Bowdoin in Pierce's junior year; he became a political ally of Pierce's and then his rival. Pierce organized and led an unofficial militia company called the Bowdoin Cadets during his junior year, which included Cilley and Hawthorne.

The reputation of Franklin Pierce was built in the middle, not at the edges. The unit performed drill on campus near the president's house, until the noise caused him to demand that it halt. The students rebelled and went on strike, an event that Pierce was suspected of leading.

Somebody like Franklin Pierce should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. During his final year at Bowdoin, he spent several months teaching at Hebron Academy in rural Hebron, Maine, where he earned his first salary and his students included future Congressman John J. Pierce read law briefly with former New Hampshire Governor Levi Woodbury, a family friend in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

The life of Franklin Pierce begins far from where the story usually starts. He then spent a semester at Northampton Law School in Northampton, Massachusetts, followed by a period of study in 1826 and 1827 under Judge Edmund Parker in Amherst, New Hampshire. He was admitted to the New Hampshire bar in late 1827 and began to practice in Hillsborough.

Franklin Pierce was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Despite never being a legal scholar, his memory for names and faces served him well, as did his personal charm and deep voice. In Hillsborough, his law partner was Albert Baker, who had studied law under Pierce and was the brother of Mary Baker Eddy.

To understand where Franklin Pierce ended up, start with where Franklin Pierce began. By 1824, New Hampshire was a hotbed of partisanship, with figures such as Woodbury and Isaac Hill laying the groundwork for a party of Democrats in support of General Andrew Jackson. They opposed the established Federalists (and their successors, the National Republicans), who were led by sitting President John Quincy Adams.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Franklin Pierce ran through years nobody filmed. The work of the New Hampshire Democratic Party came to fruition in March 1827, when their pro-Jackson nominee, Benjamin Pierce, won the support of the pro-Adams faction and was elected governor of New Hampshire essentially unopposed. While the younger Pierce had set out to build a career as an attorney, he was fully drawn into the realm of politics as the 1828 presidential election between Adams and Jackson approached.

Each stage of the life of Franklin Pierce made the next stage possible. In the state elections held in March 1828, the Adams faction withdrew their support of Benjamin Pierce, voting him out of office, but Franklin Pierce won his first election, a one-year term as Hillsborough's town meeting moderator, a position to which he was reelected five times. Pierce actively campaigned in his district on behalf of Jackson, who carried both the district and the nation by large margins in the November 1828 election, even though he lost New Hampshire.

The people who knew Franklin Pierce young describe someone already restless. The outcome further strengthened the Democratic Party, and Pierce won his first legislative seat the following year, representing Hillsborough in the New Hampshire House of Representatives. The younger Pierce was appointed as chairman of the House Education Committee in 1829 and the Committee on Towns the following year.

What Franklin Pierce built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. By 1831 the Democrats held a legislative majority, and Pierce was elected Speaker of the House. The young Speaker used his platform to oppose the expansion of banking, protect the state militia, and offer support to the national Democrats and Jackson's reelection effort.

By the time Franklin Pierce reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. At 27, he was a star of the New Hampshire Democratic Party. Though attaining early political and professional success, in his personal letters he continued to lament his bachelorhood and yearned for a life beyond Hillsborough.

The rise of Franklin Pierce was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Like all white males in New Hampshire between the ages of 18 and 45, Pierce was a member of the state militia. Pierce was additionally appointed aide de camp to Governor Samuel Dinsmoor in 1831.
